title: Detection and identification of plant diseases

notes.definition: Plant diseases are detected by visible signs such as stunted growth, spots on leaves, rot, growths, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration and the presence of pests. The cause can then be identified using a gardening manual or website, laboratory testing, or testing kits containing monoclonal antibodies.
explanation: Plants can be infected by a range of viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens, as well as by insects. At GCSE you need to know three examples: tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), a viral disease; black spot, a fungal disease of roses; and aphids, which are insect pests. Plant diseases matter because they reduce crop yields and can kill plants, affecting food supplies and the whole ecosystem.

Plant diseases can be detected by looking for signs: stunted growth; spots on leaves; areas of decay (rot); growths (such as lumps or galls); malformed stems or leaves; discolouration (for example yellowing or a mosaic pattern); and the presence of pests such as aphids. Many diseases have similar signs, so detecting that a plant is unhealthy is not the same as knowing what the cause is.

Tobacco mosaic virus infects many plants, including tomatoes. It causes a distinctive mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves, where parts of the leaves become pale. These areas have less chlorophyll, so the plant photosynthesises less and its growth is stunted. Black spot is a fungus that causes purple or black spots on rose leaves. The leaves often turn yellow and drop early, which reduces photosynthesis and growth. Aphids are small insects that feed on sap from the phloem using their mouthparts, weakening the plant; they can also carry viruses from plant to plant.

Once a disease is detected, the cause must be identified so the right treatment can be used. Identification can be made by referring to a gardening manual or website, which shows pictures and descriptions of signs. Infected plants can be taken to a laboratory, where scientists identify the pathogen. Testing kits containing monoclonal antibodies can be used in the field or the lab; the antibodies bind only to a specific pathogen, so they show quickly whether that pathogen is present.

Plants can also be damaged by ion deficiency conditions, which are not caused by pathogens but by a lack of mineral ions in the soil. Nitrate ions are needed for protein synthesis and therefore for growth, so nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth. Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll, so magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis: the leaves turn yellow because they lack chlorophyll. Less chlorophyll means less light is absorbed for photosynthesis, so the plant also grows less.
keyFacts: Plants can be infected by viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens and by insects.
Signs of disease: stunted growth, spots on leaves, areas of decay (rot), growths, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration, presence of pests.
Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration on leaves.
Black spot is a fungal disease causing purple or black spots on rose leaves.
Aphids are insects that feed on phloem sap and can spread viruses.
Identification: gardening manual or website, laboratory testing, or monoclonal antibody testing kits.
Nitrate ions are needed for protein synthesis and therefore growth.
Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll.
Magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis (yellowing of leaves).

keyTerms.definition: Yellowing of leaves caused by a lack of chlorophyll, for example due to magnesium deficiency.
A condition caused when a plant does not get enough of a particular mineral ion, such as nitrate or magnesium, from the soil.
Growth that is much less than normal, so the plant is small; caused for example by nitrate deficiency.
A plant virus that causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and growth.
A fungal disease of roses causing purple or black spots on leaves, which then turn yellow and drop early.
A small insect pest that feeds on plant sap from the phloem and can spread plant viruses.
A kit containing antibodies that bind to one specific pathogen, used to identify plant diseases quickly.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a deficiency
workedExamples.question: A farmer notices that the leaves of her crop plants are yellow, although there are no spots or pests. A soil test shows low levels of magnesium. Explain why the leaves are yellow and why the plants grow less.
steps: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll.
Without enough magnesium, the leaves cannot make enough chlorophyll, so they turn yellow (chlorosis).
Chlorophyll absorbs light for photosynthesis, so less photosynthesis happens.
Less glucose is made, so the plants grow less.
workedExamples.answer: Magnesium deficiency means less chlorophyll is made, causing chlorosis (yellow leaves). Less photosynthesis takes place, so growth is reduced.

workedExamples.title: Calculating percentage reduction in growth
workedExamples.question: Plants given all mineral ions grew to a mean height of 30 cm. Plants grown without nitrate grew to a mean height of 12 cm. Calculate the percentage reduction in height.

workedExamples.title: Calculating the percentage of infected plants
workedExamples.question: A gardener inspects 320 rose bushes and finds 48 with black spot. Calculate the percentage infected.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think yellow leaves always mean a plant has an infectious disease.
misconceptions.right: In fact yellowing (chlorosis) can be caused by magnesium deficiency, which is not caused by a pathogen.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think nitrate is needed to make chlorophyll and magnesium is needed for growth.
misconceptions.right: In fact nitrate ions are needed for protein synthesis and therefore growth; magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think seeing a sign such as spots is enough to identify the disease.
misconceptions.right: In fact many diseases cause similar signs, so the cause must be identified using a manual, website, laboratory or testing kit.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think aphids are pathogens like bacteria.
misconceptions.right: In fact aphids are insects (pests) that feed on phloem sap; they can also carry pathogens such as viruses between plants.

realWorld: Farmers and growers use monoclonal antibody test kits in the field to check crops for specific viruses before the disease spreads.
Gardeners use fertilisers containing nitrates and magnesium (for example Epsom salts, magnesium sulfate) to prevent stunted growth and chlorosis.
Plant health laboratories identify pathogens in samples sent by growers, helping to stop the spread of diseases such as ash dieback.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology only (not Combined Science Trilogy): detection and identification of plant diseases, and the effects of nitrate and magnesium ion deficiencies.
examTips: Learn the list of signs of plant disease; questions often ask for two or three.
Always link the ion to its job: nitrate → protein synthesis → growth; magnesium → chlorophyll → photosynthesis.
Use the word 'chlorosis' for yellowing caused by magnesium deficiency.
When asked how a disease could be identified, give the three methods: manual or website, laboratory, monoclonal antibody testing kit.
In calculations, check whether the question asks for a percentage reduction (use the difference) or a percentage of the total.
summary: Plants can be infected by viruses, bacteria, fungi and insects.
Signs include stunted growth, leaf spots, rot, growths, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration and pests.
Identification uses a manual or website, a laboratory or a monoclonal antibody kit.
TMV causes a mosaic pattern; black spot causes black spots on roses; aphids feed on phloem sap.
Nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth because nitrate is needed for protein synthesis.
Magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis because magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll.

questions.question: Which of these is a sign of plant disease?
markScheme: 1 mark: Spots on leaves
questions.explanation: Spots on leaves are a sign of disease, for example black spot on roses. The other options are normal features of healthy plants.

questions.question: Which mineral ion is needed by plants to make chlorophyll?
markScheme: 1 mark: Magnesium
questions.explanation: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll. Nitrate ions are needed for protein synthesis.

questions.question: What does nitrate deficiency cause in plants?
markScheme: 1 mark: Stunted growth
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions are needed for protein synthesis and therefore growth, so a lack of nitrate causes stunted growth.

questions.question: What type of organism is an aphid?
markScheme: 1 mark: An insect
questions.explanation: Aphids are small insects that feed on plant sap. They are pests, and can spread viruses.

questions.question: What is chlorosis?
options: Yellowing of leaves due to lack of chlorophyll
Black spots caused by a fungus
markScheme: 1 mark: Yellowing of leaves due to lack of chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Chlorosis means yellow leaves caused by too little chlorophyll, for example from magnesium deficiency.

questions.question: Which method of identifying a plant disease uses antibodies that bind to one specific pathogen?
markScheme: 1 mark: Monoclonal antibody testing kit
questions.explanation: Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one antigen, so a test kit can show whether a specific pathogen is present.

questions.question: A tomato plant has leaves with a patchy pattern of pale and dark green areas. Which disease is most likely?
markScheme: 1 mark: Tobacco mosaic virus
questions.explanation: TMV causes a distinctive mosaic pattern of discolouration. Magnesium deficiency causes general yellowing and nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth.

questions.question: Why do plants need nitrate ions?
options: For protein synthesis and therefore growth
markScheme: 1 mark: For protein synthesis and therefore growth
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions provide the nitrogen used to make amino acids and proteins, which are needed for growth.

questions.question: A plant has yellow leaves but no spots, no pests and normal-sized stems. A soil test shows normal nitrate levels. What is the most likely cause?
markScheme: 1 mark: Magnesium deficiency
questions.explanation: Yellow leaves with no pests or spots, and normal nitrate, point to chlorosis from magnesium deficiency.

questions.question: Why might a grower use a monoclonal antibody kit rather than a gardening website to identify a disease?
options: The kit can identify all diseases at once
The kit gives a specific identification of the pathogen, even when signs look similar
The kit also cures the disease
The kit works for ion deficiencies
markScheme: 1 mark: The kit gives a specific identification of the pathogen, even when signs look similar
questions.explanation: Different diseases can have similar signs. Monoclonal antibodies bind to one pathogen only, giving a reliable identification. Each kit tests for one pathogen, and kits cannot detect ion deficiencies.

questions.question:
A gardener inspects 320 rose bushes. 48 of them have black spot.
Calculate the percentage of rose bushes with black spot.

Plants given all mineral ions grew to a mean height of 30 cm. Plants grown without nitrate ions grew to a mean height of 12 cm.
Calculate the percentage reduction in height caused by nitrate deficiency.
questions.explanation: The reduction is 18 cm. 18 ÷ 30 = 0.6, so the reduction is 60%. Dividing by 12 instead of 30 is a common error.

questions.question:
A student counted the aphids on five plants: 14, 9, 22, 17 and 13.
Calculate the mean number of aphids per plant.
questions.explanation: The total is 75 aphids. 75 ÷ 5 = 15 aphids per plant.

questions.question:
The mean dry mass of plants grown with all mineral ions was 25.0 g. The mean dry mass of plants grown without magnesium ions was 18.5 g.
Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass.
questions.explanation: Decrease = 6.5 g. 6.5 ÷ 25.0 = 0.26, so 26%. Less chlorophyll means less photosynthesis, so less biomass is made.

questions.question: Give three signs that a plant may have a disease.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three from: stunted growth; spots on leaves; areas of decay/rot; growths; malformed stems or leaves; discolouration; presence of pests
questions.explanation: These are the seven signs listed in the specification.

questions.question: Give two ways a gardener could identify the disease affecting a plant.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: refer to a gardening manual or website; take the plant to a laboratory to identify the pathogen; use a testing kit containing monoclonal antibodies
questions.explanation: Detection (noticing signs) comes first; identification finds the actual cause.

questions.question: Name the type of pathogen that causes black spot on roses.
markScheme: 1 mark: fungus
questions.explanation: Black spot is a fungal disease.

questions.question: Explain why a plant lacking nitrate ions shows stunted growth.
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrate ions are needed for protein synthesis
1 mark: proteins are needed for growth (making new cells), so less growth
questions.explanation: Without nitrate, the plant cannot make enough protein to build new cells, so it grows less.

questions.question: Explain why a plant lacking magnesium ions has yellow leaves and grows poorly.
markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll
1 mark: less chlorophyll so leaves are yellow (chlorosis)
1 mark: less light absorbed so less photosynthesis/glucose, so less growth
questions.explanation: The chain of reasoning is magnesium → chlorophyll → photosynthesis → glucose → growth.

questions.question: Describe how tobacco mosaic virus affects the growth of a plant.
markScheme: 1 mark: causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration on leaves, where parts lack chlorophyll
1 mark: so less photosynthesis, reducing growth
questions.explanation: Discoloured areas have less chlorophyll, so the plant makes less glucose.

questions.question: Explain why it is important to identify the cause of a plant disease rather than just detecting the signs.
markScheme: 1 mark: different causes can produce similar signs (e.g. yellow leaves from TMV, black spot or magnesium deficiency)
1 mark: different causes need different treatments / so the correct treatment or control can be used
questions.explanation: A fungicide would not help a magnesium deficiency, and fertiliser would not cure a virus.

questions.question: Aphids feed on phloem sap. Suggest two ways that an aphid infestation could harm a plant.
markScheme: 1 mark: removes sugars/dissolved food from the phloem, so less is available for growth
1 mark: can carry/transmit viruses (pathogens) into the plant
questions.explanation: Aphids are both a direct problem (removing sap) and a vector for viral diseases.

questions.question: A farmer sees stunted plants in one field. Suggest how she could find out whether this is caused by a pathogen or by nitrate deficiency.
markScheme: 1 mark: test the soil for nitrate levels / add nitrate fertiliser to some plants and see if they recover
1 mark: send samples to a laboratory or use a monoclonal antibody kit to test for pathogens
1 mark: look for other signs such as spots, rot, growths or pests that indicate a pathogen
questions.explanation: Stunted growth has several possible causes, so the farmer needs tests that separate them.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of using a gardening website to identify a plant disease, compared with sending a sample to a laboratory.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage: quicker / cheaper / easy for anyone to use
1 mark: disadvantage: less reliable, because many diseases have similar signs, so it may be misidentified
questions.explanation: A laboratory identifies the actual pathogen, which is more reliable but slower and costs more.

questions.question: Describe how plant diseases can be detected and identified.
markScheme: Indicative content: detection by signs: stunted growth, spots on leaves, areas of decay/rot, growths, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration, presence of pests; identification by: gardening manual or website, taking infected plants to a laboratory to identify the pathogen, testing kits containing monoclonal antibodies.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several signs described AND at least two methods of identification.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some signs or methods listed, with only detection or only identification covered.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The question has two parts: detecting (signs) and identifying (methods). Cover both.

questions.question:
A student grew three groups of seedlings in solutions: A with all mineral ions, B without nitrate ions, and C without magnesium ions. After four weeks: A plants were tall with green leaves; B plants were very small with few leaves; C plants were of medium height with yellow leaves.
Describe and explain the results.
markScheme: Indicative content: A is the control with healthy growth; B shows stunted growth; nitrate ions are needed for protein synthesis; proteins are needed for growth/new cells; so without nitrate growth is stunted; C shows chlorosis (yellow leaves); magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; less chlorophyll so less light absorbed; less photosynthesis so less glucose; so growth reduced (medium height); comparison with control shows effect is due to the missing ion; control variables (light, temperature, volume of solution).
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): describes the results for all groups and gives detailed explanations for both deficiencies, linking ion → molecule → process → growth.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes results and explains at least one deficiency correctly.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description of the results with little or no explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers name chlorosis and stunted growth and explain each through the role of the ion.

questions.question: Compare the effects of tobacco mosaic virus and magnesium deficiency on a plant.
markScheme: Indicative content: both cause discolouration of leaves; both reduce chlorophyll so reduce photosynthesis and growth; TMV is caused by a pathogen (virus) and is infectious, spreading between plants; magnesium deficiency is caused by lack of an ion in the soil and is not infectious; TMV gives a mosaic pattern; magnesium deficiency gives chlorosis (general yellowing); magnesium deficiency can be treated with fertiliser, TMV cannot be cured in this way.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear similarities and differences given.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple points about one or both with little comparison.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A comparison needs both similarities and differences; the key difference is infectious pathogen versus lack of a mineral ion.

questions.question: Name the type of pathogen that causes tobacco mosaic disease.
markScheme: 1 mark: virus
questions.explanation: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) is a plant virus.
